newsitem.title: USA: OUTLOOK: All eyes hungry for U.S. distillate data.
newsitem.headline: OUTLOOK: All eyes hungry for U.S. distillate data.

text.p: U.S. products traders will focus this week on distillate inventory data as October arrives and the real countdown to the heating season begins amid the lowest late-September stocks in a generation.

"If this was the beginning of September, people could shrug off inventory numbers. But it's now the end of September and the heating season is about to begin," said John Lichtblau, president of the Petroleum Industry Research Foundation.

"Inventories are very low for this time of year so if there is no significant U.S. build there will be further price moves," he said, noting East Coast heating oil prices are now aloft at about 72 cents a gallon, 20 cents over a year ago.
The latest American Petroleum Institute (API) estimates pegged total U.S. distillate stocks at 112.4 million barrels for the week ending September 20, 15 percent lower than the same week of 1995.
"We haven't seen stocks this low since at least the early 1970's," said senior API analyst Jim Lockhart. The API is set to release new weekly stocks data late Tuesday afteroon.
Traders will then shift their sights Wednesday to their price beacon, weekly data from the Energy Information Administration.

Jet fuel prices, pegged off NYMEX heat futures, have skyrocketed in tandem with heating oil, with spot New York Harbor aviation-quality 54-grade fuel reaching a stratospheric 71.78 cents a gallon on Sept. 27, versus a more earth-bound 53.18 cents this time last year.
Although absolute prices remain sky-high, differentials plunged by two cents a gallon in New York Harbor late last week and by 1.25 cents on the Gulf Coast.
Jet fuel traders said supplies are beginning to far outstrip demand, as refineries begin producing more distillates, and, as a consequence, more jet fuel as well.
"We're making a whole lot of jet fuel but the high travel season is over and demand is off," one New York jet fuel trader said, predicting diffs could come under more downward pressure this week.

In the Midwest, low sulphur diesel prices are expected to firm on increased agricultural demand as drier weather moves into the region, allowing farmers to resume autumn corn and sorghum harvests delayed by rain last week.
"We could see some firmness on low sulphur diesel as the fields dry out and we see more harvest activity," a midwestern trader in Kansas City, Missouri said.
Midcontinent unleaded gasoline prices are expected to ease, although unleaded will draw some support from outages at three key regional refineries, traders said.

Outages were affecting crude throughput at Farmland Industries Inc's 68,600 barrel per day (bpd) Coffeyville refinery and National Cooperative Refinery Association's 75,600 bpd McPherson refinery, and a catalytic cracker was taken down for month-long turnaround at Conoco's 140,000 barrel per day Ponca City, Oklahoma, refinery, traders said.
-- Ransdell Pierson, New York Energy Desk 212 859-1632
